strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely important and underexplored problem in open-vocabulary 3DSG generation: noise from occlusions and constrained viewpoints propagating into cross-image aggregation. The proposed re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a sensible and reasonably novel solution — rendering best-view images from reconstructed object point clouds (with a principled view-quality score combining visibility, uprightness, and prior alignment) and using caption agreement as an uncertainty signal.

The object-level RAG mechanism is a clean idea: using the partially constructed 3DSG as a retrieval database where low-uncertainty objects provide context for refining high-uncertainty captions. The ablation (random-RAG vs. semantic-aware retrieval) supports the design choice.

The dynamic downsample-mapping strategy is simple but effective, yielding a substantial ~2.7x speedup in mapping time (6.65s/iter to 2.49s/iter) while maintaining comparable semantic segmentation accuracy (best mAcc of 40.67), addressing the practical runtime bottleneck of open-vocabulary pipelines.

Comprehensive ablation studies with per-scene heatmaps (Figure 5, A.5) show each component contributes, with the re-shot uncertainty estimation providing the largest gains. The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the pipeline is described with sufficient implementation detail (checkpoints, models, hyperparameters, prompts, pseudo-code in appendix).
Reproducibility considerations are good: code and evaluation scripts are promised, datasets are public, and prompts/hyperparameters are documented.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to Replica, a synthetic, static, well-lit indoor dataset. The motivating claims emphasize occlusion, constrained viewpoints, and safety-critical robotics — conditions much more prevalent in real-world data — yet no experiments on real datasets (e.g., ScanNet, HM3D, or a robot platform) are provided. This weakens the case that the method's benefits transfer beyond clean synthetic scenes.

The uncertainty measure is ad hoc: cosine similarity between CLIP caption embeddings is a heuristic proxy, not a calibrated uncertainty estimate. Key design choices — the top-50% low/high uncertainty split, the top-1 cluster selection, thresholds δsim, α=β=0.2 — lack sensitivity analysis or justification, and behavior when all or no captions agree with the re-shot is not discussed.

Baseline coverage in the main comparison (Table 1) is narrow: only ConceptGraphs and its detector variant. Stronger or more recent open-vocabulary/open-set 3DSG methods (e.g., Open3DSG, Clio, HOV-SG, Hydra) are not compared on scene graph metrics, making it hard to assess state-of-the-art positioning.

The edge precision comparison is not strictly apples-to-apples: the authors change the relation space (five to eight categories plus few-shot prompts), so improved edge precision partially reflects a different task definition rather than only the noise-reduction contribution. This should be disentangled.

The ablation of Figure 3 differs from the segmentation protocol of Section 4.3 by relying on GPT-4o as a 'semantic assigner' of GT labels to predicted nodes; this introduces another LLM in the evaluation loop whose error characteristics are unanalyzed, and some ablation deltas are modest.

Heavy dependence on closed-source commercial models (GPT-4-0613, GPT-4o-mini) raises reproducibility, cost, and API-stability concerns; the added re-shot rendering, extra VLM captioning, clustering, and refinement calls likely increase overall pipeline cost, and only mapping time is reported — an end-to-end runtime/compute comparison is missing.

Human evaluation protocol is under-specified: number of annotators, per-annotator agreement, inter-annotator reliability, and blinding procedures are not reported, and annotators may systematically favor longer or more structured captions, potentially biasing comparisons.

No explicit limitations section; failure modes (e.g., poor reconstruction quality invalidating re-shot images, retrieval propagating incorrect context, dynamic voxel sizing distorting the NN-ratio matching) are not analyzed.
The improvement in semantic segmentation is partly offset by lower f-mIoU than OpenMask3D (35.65 vs. 49.26), so 'comparable or even superior accuracy' should be stated more carefully.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and practically important problem: noisy per-image captions (from occlusion and constrained viewpoints) propagating into cross-image aggregation in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph generation. The safety-critical motivation is well articulated.

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a sensible idea: rendering best-view images from reconstructed object point clouds and using caption agreement with crop captions as an uncertainty proxy is intuitive and well motivated by optimal-viewpoint literature.
Reported gains are substantial: node precision 0.82 vs 0.68 (ConceptGraphs) and edge precision 0.91 vs 0.82, with reduced duplicates, across 8 Replica scenes.
The dynamic downsampling strategy is simple but effective, cutting mapping time roughly two-thirds while maintaining competitive segmentation accuracy (best mAcc in Table 2).

Ablations (Figure 3) cover all major components including a random-retrieval control, and the case study in Figure 6 illustrates the failure mode the method addresses. The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with reproducibility details (checkpoints, hyperparameters, prompts) and a promised code release.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the primary baseline. The pipeline is an incremental extension of ConceptGraphs: dynamic voxel downsampling (Eq. 1) is a straightforward heuristic, the fusion similarity largely follows Gu et al. (2024) with a modified NN threshold, and 'object-level RAG' amounts to retrieving the spatially nearest caption and feeding a stitched image to a VLM. Best-view rendering is a classical technique. The claim of being 'the first to specifically address noise in cross-image information aggregation' is overstated given related uncertainty/filtering work in the mapping literature.

Evaluation is confined to a single synthetic dataset (Replica, 8 clean indoor rooms). No real-world benchmarks such as ScanNet or HM3D are evaluated, despite the paper's motivation being robustness to imperfect real-world viewing conditions — precisely the setting where the proposed noise-robustness claims should be tested.

The main Table 1 relies on human evaluation by 'knowledgeable university students' with insufficient methodological detail: number of annotators, annotator overlap, inter-annotator agreement, whether evaluators were blinded to method identity, and sample sizes per cell are unreported. Caption style differences between methods could make blind evaluation fragile, and no automatic LLM-based or similarity-based node/edge metric corroborates Table 1.

Baseline coverage in Table 1 is narrow (only ConceptGraphs and ConceptGraphs-Detector). Other open-vocabulary/open-set 3DSG methods discussed in related work (e.g., HOV-SG/Werby et al., Open3DSG, Clio) are not compared on scene graph quality.

Heavy dependence on proprietary models (gpt-4-0613, gpt-4o-mini, GPT-4o as semantic assigner in the ablation) creates reproducibility, cost, and version-drift concerns. The method's uncertainty estimate is itself a function of the VLM, and no analysis of sensitivity to the VLM choice is given in the main text (the case study uses LLaVA, but main results do not).

Efficiency claims are incomplete: the two-thirds reduction applies only to the mapping stage, while the proposed method adds re-shot rendering, view scoring, clustering, extra VLM calls for refinement, and RAG retrieval. End-to-end pipeline runtime and API cost versus ConceptGraphs are not reported, so the overall accuracy-efficiency trade-off is unclear.

Inconsistency between evaluation protocols: the full pipeline scores f-mIoU 35.65 in Table 2 but 54.26 in Figure 3, and the ablation protocol (GPT-4o as semantic assigner on final captions) differs from Section 4.3. This makes cross-table comparison confusing and weakens confidence in the quantitative story.

No downstream task evaluation. The introduction motivates the work via manipulation/navigation and safety-critical scenarios, but the experiments never test whether the improved 3DSGs actually help any downstream task.

The object-level RAG design is simplistic: retrieval is purely 3D-position-based nearest neighbor, the 'document' is the top-50% of objects by a heuristic uncertainty score, and the composite re-shot+crop image prompt is ad hoc; there is no analysis of failure cases of the refinement itself (e.g., when the re-shot caption is wrong and the retrieved context reinforces the error).

strengths: Identifies a genuine and practically important problem: noise in cross-image information aggregation for open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs (constrained viewpoints, occlusion), with a clear motivating example and safety-relevant framing.

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a sensible and reasonably novel idea: rendering best-view images from reconstructed object point clouds (via a multi-term view quality score) and using caption agreement as an uncertainty proxy is a clean way to filter unreliable captions without retraining.

The object-level RAG mechanism (low-uncertainty objects forming a retrieval document used to refine high-uncertainty captions) is an interesting adaptation of retrieval-augmented generation to spatial scene graphs.

Dynamic downsample-mapping is a simple but effective efficiency contribution, with a reported ~2.7x speedup in mapping time at comparable mAcc/f-mIoU, and it is consistently integrated into fusion and edge construction (dynamic NN-ratio threshold).

Ablation study covers all main components, including a random-retrieval control that isolates the value of semantic-aware retrieval; per-scene heatmaps and a qualitative case study are provided in the appendix.

Reproducibility statement is concrete (checkpoints, backbones, prompts, hyperparameters, promised code release), and relevant prior work (ConceptGraphs, ConceptFusion, Clio, Open3DSG, etc.) is appropriately credited.
Honest disclosure of LLM usage for writing assistance and a brief ethics statement.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single synthetic dataset (Replica), which is clean, static, and idealized. Claims of robustness to real-world noise (occlusion, poor imaging) are exactly the claims that require evaluation on real data (e.g., ScanNet, HM3D, or robot-captured sequences), but none is provided. This substantially weakens the generalization argument.

The headline results (Table 1) rest on human annotation with too little methodological detail: number of annotators per unit, inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa), instructions, and how disagreements were resolved are unreported. Without these, precision differences of 0.14–0.24 are hard to interpret.

Comparison in Table 1 is restricted to ConceptGraphs and ConceptGraphs-Detector. Other published systems measured on similar setups (e.g., Clio, OpenMask3D, Open3DSG) appear only in the segmentation table, and edge-precision gains may be confounded by the changed relation taxonomy and few-shot prompting rather than by the proposed uncertainty mechanism; there is no edge-level ablation.

There is a large, under-explained discrepancy between Table 2 (f-mIoU 35.65 for the full pipeline) and the ablation in Figure 3 (f-mIoU 54.26 for full pipeline, 35.56 for w/o Reshot). Although the protocols differ (fused embeddings vs. caption-based assignment via GPT-4o), the paper does not explain why the numbers differ so much, which undermines confidence in the ablation conclusions.

The uncertainty proxy is heuristic and unvalidated: 'uncertainty = 1 - CLIP caption similarity' is not calibrated, the re-shot caption itself can be wrong (rendered point-cloud images lack realistic texture and context, potentially biasing the VLM), and key design choices (top-50% document threshold, alpha = beta = 0.2, clustering procedure) are not ablated.

Heavy dependence on proprietary closed-source models (gpt-4-0613, gpt-4o-mini) for both the pipeline and the ablation's semantic assigner raises reproducibility, cost, and result-stability concerns; no open-model comparison is given in the main results, and API drift could prevent exact reproduction.

Runtime accounting is incomplete: the paper reports speedup for the mapping stage only, while re-shot rendering, best-view scoring, and additional VLM/LLM calls plausibly increase captioning latency; a full end-to-end time comparison is needed to substantiate the efficiency claim.

The dynamic downsampling rule (voxel size proportional to the square root of the bounding-box diagonal) and the dynamic NN-ratio threshold are plausible heuristics, but their effect is not independently disentangled from other components, and the stated ambition of 'finer granularity and higher efficiency without trade-off' is asserted more than demonstrated.

Some overclaiming in writing (e.g., 'we are the first to specifically address noise in cross-image aggregation') and minor presentation issues ('lack-sampled', 'Retireve' in Figure 1, typos) suggest the manuscript would benefit from another careful pass.

Contribution type: no explicit type is declared; assessed as Algorithms/General. Under that framing the algorithmic novelty is moderate (heuristic uncertainty scoring plus applied RAG over an existing ConceptGraphs-style pipeline), which is acceptable, but the evidence base (single synthetic dataset, thin evaluation protocol) is on the light side for that framing.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies a genuine weakness in open-vocabulary 3DSG pipelines (noisy cross-image aggregation of captions under occlusion/constrained viewpoints) and frames a sensible 'diagnose-then-rectify' paradigm.

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a reasonably original mechanism: rendering an optimal 'best-view' re-shot from the reconstructed geometry and measuring caption consistency against passive observations is a simple but effective way to quantify per-object semantic ambiguity, and it goes beyond prior passive best-frame-selection methods.

Comprehensive experimental evidence for an Applied/Systems contribution: two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D) with a fair adoption of the OpenFunGraph protocol, a stress test with injected pose noise, an ablation over all proposed components (including a 'random RAG' control), a runtime analysis, and an actual robotic deployment.

The human evaluation on Replica is conducted with a strict annotation protocol, three independent annotators, and reported inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.76), which is more rigorous than typical qualitative assessments in this area.
Both an open-source (LLaVA-v1.5-7b) and a closed (GPT-4o) variant are reported, which helps disentangle framework gains from raw model capacity, and practical costs (~$0.50/scene) are documented.
weaknesses: Key methodological details are underspecified in the main text: the construction of the consensus caption c-hat, the exact clustering procedure and reliability score s-hat over the k caption similarities (Eq. 3), and the moving-average embedding update are only described qualitatively; the reproducibility of the core uncertainty mechanism is therefore hard to assess.

The strongest available baseline (OpenFunGraph) is not included in the human evaluation, which only compares against ConceptGraphs variants; the claim of cleaner, more precise graphs is thus not verified against the closest competitor.

Some quantitative gains are narrower than the narrative suggests: the open-source Ours-LLaVA variant actually falls below OpenFunGraph on several SceneFun3D metrics (e.g., Objects R@3 81.3 vs. 81.8; Edges R@5 87.1 vs. 88.1), and edge gains on FunGraph3D are marginal (65.7 vs. 65.1 R@5; 91.4 R@10 ties), so the 'substantial margins' claim mostly holds for the GPT-4o variant on node classification.

The 'active verification' framing is somewhat overstated: the re-shot is a passive offline rendering from a reconstructed point cloud, not active exploration; the dependence of the best-view selection (Eq. 2 weights, α_vis = 0.6) on the prior viewpoint term limits the claimed freedom from 'unseen backsides', and the approach remains an offline system despite the robotics motivation.

Potential circularity in the RAG design is not fully addressed: low-uncertainty objects serve both as ground truth for themselves (caption set to c-hat) and as retrieval anchors for high-uncertainty objects, so systematic errors among confident objects could propagate; the ablation does not isolate this risk.

The ablation and human evaluation are conducted only on Replica (a clean, synthetic-grade dataset), while the noisy-pose stress test results are confined to a narrow noise regime (sigma_trans = 0.02 m, sigma_rot = 1 degree); robustness claims would be stronger with ablations on the noisier real-world benchmarks.

The paper lacks a limitations discussion, mentions no code release, and contains polish issues (raw LaTeX labels in the text, typos such as 'Celling' and 'Higer Score'), which slightly undermines confidence in overall rigor.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and well-motivated: shifting from passive 'best-of-captured-views' frame selection to an active, geometry-guided 're-shot' verification step is a genuinely different angle on the well-known cross-view aggregation noise problem in open-vocabulary 3DSG construction, and the diagnose-then-rectify framing (uncertainty estimation followed by object-level RAG refinement) is coherent.

The experimental program is unusually broad for this area: two real-world benchmarks following an established protocol (OpenFunGraph), a noise-injection stress test on camera poses, a human evaluation with a documented annotation protocol and Fleiss' Kappa agreement check, component ablations, and a physical robot deployment on real hardware.

The ablation study (Fig. 3) is informative: it separates the contribution of re-shot uncertainty estimation, RAG, random vs. spatial retrieval, and re-shot image concatenation, with 'w/o Reshot' showing the largest drop, which supports the paper's central claim.

Runtime/cost analysis (dynamic downsampling giving ~2.7x fusion speedup over ConceptGraphs, per-scene API cost) and honest acknowledgment that the system is currently offline are useful practical details.
weaknesses: The state-of-the-art claim rests heavily on the GPT-4o variant, which conflates model capacity with the proposed method: on SceneFun3D, Ours-LLaVA (the capacity-controlled comparison) actually loses to OpenFunGraph on most metrics (81.3 vs. 81.8 R@3 nodes; 87.1 vs. 88.1 R@5 edges; 95.8 vs. 96.2 R@10 edges), and edge gains on FunGraph3D are marginal (65.7 vs. 65.1 R@5; 91.4 vs. 91.4 R@10). With a matched open-weight VLM, the contribution does not consistently beat the strongest baseline.

There is a potential circularity/evaluation-bias concern: GPT-4o is used both as the reasoning backbone of Ours-GPT and as the 'semantic assigner' judging caption correctness in the Replica ablations (Sec. 4.4). GPT captions being judged by GPT may inflate the ablation results, and no counterbalancing or non-GPT judge is reported.

The uncertainty estimate itself is heuristic and not validated: it is derived from CLIP cosine similarity between one VLM caption of a single rendered re-shot and the passive captions. The re-shot caption is generated by the same fallible VLM and inherits any upstream segmentation/fusion errors (e.g., an object mask that incorrectly merged two objects would produce a confidently wrong re-shot). No calibration analysis or measure of the uncertainty score's reliability (e.g., correlation with actual caption errors) is provided.

The 'RAG' component is quite thin relative to the framing: retrieval is simply the nearest low-uncertainty object by 3D position, providing a single neighbor caption as context. The breadth of novelty over existing caption-aggregation + refinement pipelines should be stated more modestly.

The human evaluation compares only against ConceptGraphs/CG-D on 8 Replica scenes, omitting OpenFunGraph, the strongest automated baseline; and the ablations are run only on synthetic Replica rather than the real-world benchmarks where the main claims are made.

Some overclaiming in the writing ('hallucination-free', 'rigorously quantify', 'exceptional resilience') is not fully supported by the evidence, and the noise-injection test (sigma_trans = 0.02 m, sigma_rot = 1 deg) is described as an 'extreme stress test' despite being a rather mild perturbation by SLAM standards.

Clarity issues: the caption-clustering step for the consensus caption c-hat and final score s-hat is described only loosely (clustering criteria, how s-hat is computed), and Eq. (1)'s dimensional scaling is asserted rather than justified; key details are deferred to supplementary material, making the main paper hard to fully reproduce.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and well-motivated problem in open-vocabulary 3DSG construction: semantic inconsistency arising from constrained viewpoints and occlusion during cross-image aggregation. The proposed 'diagnose-then-rectify' paradigm is a sensible and reasonably original framing.

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a novel and conceptually appealing contribution: leveraging reconstructed geometry to actively render an optimal verification viewpoint transforms passive frame selection into active verification. The view-scoring design (visibility, horizon alignment, prior-viewpoint consistency) is simple, lightweight, and clearly explained.

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D) under a published protocol, a noisy-pose stress test, a fine-grained human evaluation with a strict annotation protocol and inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa = 0.76), component ablations, runtime/cost analysis, and an actual physical robot deployment. This exceeds the typical evidence bar for applied robotics/vision systems work.

Fairness is partly addressed by evaluating both a closed model variant (GPT-4o) and an open-weight variant (LLaVA-1.5-7b), showing gains persist even with a weak captioner (73.6% vs 70.7% R@3 for OpenFunGraph), which strengthens the claim that the framework, not raw model capacity, drives the improvements.

The ablations are meaningful: removing the re-shot module causes the largest degradation, and replacing position-based retrieval with random retrieval degrades performance, supporting the necessity of both the uncertainty filter and the semantic-anchor retrieval.
Reproducibility-relevant details are provided: hyperparameters, model versions, prompts (partially), and cost figures, with additional material deferred to the supplementary.
weaknesses: Several core components are heuristic rather than principled. The uncertainty score is a CLIP caption-embedding similarity with clustering of unknown granularity, the 50% low-uncertainty cut-off is arbitrary, and the view-scoring weights (αprior = αhoriz = 0.2, αvis = 0.6) appear hand-tuned. Sensitivity analyses are deferred to the supplementary, so the robustness of these design choices cannot be judged from the main text.

The ablation study is conducted only on Replica, a clean synthetic dataset, whereas the main SOTA claims are made on real-world data (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D). It is unclear whether the component conclusions transfer to the noisier real-world settings where the method is claimed to help most.

The Ours-GPT variant uses GPT-4o while most baselines rely on weaker or open models; the headline gains partially reflect captioner capacity. Although the LLaVA variant mitigates this, GPT-4o-based numbers should be interpreted as an upper bound, and the paper's 'new state-of-the-art' claim rests substantially on them.

Potential evaluation circularity: GPT-4o is used both as the captioner/refiner in the pipeline and as the semantic assigner in the Replica ablation evaluation, which could bias caption matching in favor of the method's outputs. This concern is not discussed.

The object-level RAG is quite simple: retrieving only the single nearest object caption and concatenating two images. The framing as 'Retrieval-Augmented Generation' somewhat oversells a nearest-neighbor context lookup; a comparison against more retrieval candidates or richer context would clarify whether the design is sufficient or merely minimal.

Gains on edges are modest (e.g., 65.7% vs 65.1% R@5 on FunGraph3D) and the relation space is expanded relative to baselines; although BERT-embedding mapping is used to reduce mapping bias, the evaluation protocol difference introduces some uncertainty about edge-level comparability.

The dynamic downsampling strategy (Eq. 1), while claimed to improve efficiency and re-identification, is not independently ablated; its contribution to accuracy versus runtime is not separated from the re-shot/RAG components.

The dependency on accurate reconstruction and poses is acknowledged, but only a single noise configuration is tested; the boundary conditions under which re-shot rendering fails (e.g., very sparse or heavily incomplete objects, outdoor scenes) are not characterized. Robustness claims like 'exceptional resilience' and 'nearly eliminating duplicate node predictions' are stronger than the evidence strictly supports.

Writing and presentation issues: raw LaTeX macros appear in Eq. (1) in the compiled text ('\label {eq:voxel_size}'), there are typos (e.g., 'Higer Score' in Fig. 2, 'Celling' in Fig. 4), and strong priority claims ('We are the first to address semantic inconsistency in cross-view aggregation') are somewhat overstated given prior filtering/best-view work [6,14,20]. No explicit statement about code release is given, which limits reproducibility given the many heuristic components.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem (semantic noise from occlusions/constrained viewpoints in cross-image aggregation for open-vocabulary 3DSG construction) with a coherent 'diagnose-then-rectify' framework that combines active re-shot verification with object-level contextual refinement.

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a sensible and reasonably novel mechanism: comparing passive crop captions against actively rendered best-view captions provides an interpretable reliability score, and the multi-factor view scoring (visibility, horizon, prior consistency) is well justified and analyzed qualitatively in the supplementary.

Experimental evidence is extensive: SOTA comparisons on two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D) under a standard protocol, a rigorous human evaluation on Replica with three annotators and reported Fleiss' Kappa, component ablations, RAG retrieval-size ablations, pose-noise and point-density stress tests, runtime/cost analysis, and an actual physical robot deployment with a quantitative real-world human evaluation against ConceptGraphs.

The mechanism analysis is convincing: the isolated re-shot variant (Re-shot VLM) degrading drastically, and the 'Ours Node + CG Edge' variant showing edge gains driven by node quality, give good insight into where the improvements come from. Hyperparameter studies in the supplementary are thorough and justify design choices with clear trade-off discussions.
Reproducibility support is decent: implementation details, hyperparameters, algorithmic pseudo-code, and complete prompt templates are provided.
The work is honest about its offline nature and situates itself within decoupled robotic architectures; limitations regarding reliance on 3D reconstruction quality are probed rather than ignored.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely systems/prompt-engineering integration of existing components (SAM, CLIP, VLM/LLM captioning, view rendering, retrieval) rather than a new algorithmic or theoretical advance. The 'RAG' terminology is somewhat inflated: the retrieval is a nearest-neighbor lookup by 3D position of the single nearest low-uncertainty object, which is a simple heuristic rather than learned or semantically driven retrieval. The paper would benefit from more explicit positioning as an Applied/Systems contribution.

The uncertainty estimation is a hand-crafted heuristic (cosine similarity of CLIP embeddings of captions, KMeans with fixed K=3, consensus-cluster mean) with no calibration analysis, no validation that the scores correlate with true semantic error beyond end-task metrics, and no comparison against alternative uncertainty estimators (e.g., embedding variance across views, evidential approaches). This is a substantive gap given that uncertainty estimation is the paper's core novelty.

Potential evaluation circularity: key hyperparameters (δ_sample, δ_sim, scoring weights) are selected based on analyses performed on Replica, which is also the dataset used for the human evaluation and the main ablations. This raises overfitting-to-evaluation-data concerns, and ablations are only conducted on Replica (simulated) rather than on the real-world benchmarks.

Fairness and generality of the edge evaluation are only partially convincing: the relation space is intentionally constrained to eight categories with few-shot LLM prompting, which is not fully open-vocabulary; the BERT-embedding-based predicate mapping mitigates but does not eliminate mapping bias concerns. Baseline comparisons also mix backbone strengths (GPT-4o vs. LLaVA), and while the Passive VLM control partially addresses this, some reported gains may still reflect VLM capacity rather than the proposed mechanism.

The robustness claims are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence: the injected pose noise (σ_trans = 0.02 m, σ_rot = 1°) and density perturbations are relatively mild, and 'exceptional resilience' language is stronger than what a single noise level can establish. The real-robot deployment lacks a direct comparison table in the main text (results appear only in the supplementary with a single baseline).
No explicit statement of code/data release, which limits reproducibility for a pipeline with many prompt-engineered and hyperparameter-dependent stages.

Minor presentation issues: some hyperbolic phrasing ('profound resilience', 'first to address'), the odd 'Passive VLM (gpt-5.2)' entry in Table 1 is unexplained, and Table 1 leaves missing cells for the Ours Node + CG Edge node results without explanation.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely important and well-articulated problem: semantic inconsistency in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph construction caused by occlusion and constrained viewpoints, and the motivation (safety-critical robotic use) is compelling.

The 'diagnose-then-rectify' framing—active re-shot verification followed by uncertainty-guided contextual rectification—is a coherent and reasonably novel combination relative to purely passive frame-selection baselines.

The experimental evidence is extensive: quantitative comparisons against multiple SOTA baselines on two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D), a carefully documented human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' κ = 0.76), component ablations, hyperparameter sweeps in the supplementary, a pose-noise stress test, and a physical robot deployment.

The mechanism analysis (e.g., showing that isolated re-shot captioning degrades performance and that edge gains are largely driven by node quality) adds credibility and insight into why the method works.
Runtime and cost analysis is transparent, including API costs and per-object rendering overhead.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental and the contribution is closer to a well-engineered system than a new method: the 're-shot' step is essentially rendering the best view from an already-reconstructed point cloud (closely related to prior best-view selection and viewpoint-entropy works the authors cite), and the 'Object-level RAG' reduces to retrieving the single nearest neighbor's caption and pasting it into a VLM prompt. The heavy use of fashionable terminology (RAG, uncertainty, active photographer) overstates what are relatively simple heuristics.

The claim of open-vocabulary 3DSG is undermined in practice: the final edge taxonomy is deliberately constrained to eight fixed categories with few-shot prompting, and node captions are filtered through fixed heuristic rules; the graph is far less open than claimed.

The uncertainty estimation is a heuristic proxy (CLIP embedding similarity between re-shot and crop captions, KMeans with K=3, top-50% cut-off) with no validation that the scores are calibrated or meaningful as uncertainty; there is no analysis of how often the re-shot caption itself is wrong beyond a single case study, even though the authors acknowledge the re-shot can fail (e.g., transparent objects).

Key design parameters are numerous and hand-tuned (δsim, δsample, scoring weights α, K=3 clusters, top-50% ranking, k=1 retrieval), raising concerns about dataset-specific overfitting; several conclusions from the ablations appear dataset-bound (Replica-only ablations), and no code or release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility.

The headline results depend on proprietary frontier models (GPT-4o, and even a 'gpt-5.2' baseline), complicating fair comparison and reproducibility; the local LLaVA variant, while competitive, is the more scientifically meaningful result and shows smaller margins.

Human evaluation is limited to 8 Replica scenes and only against ConceptGraphs variants, not the strongest baselines (OpenFunGraph, Open3DSG); some quantitative gains are marginal (e.g., Edge R@5 65.7 vs 65.1 on FunGraph3D) and not accompanied by significance testing.

The system is fundamentally offline despite being motivated by robotics and safety-critical deployment; the online/robotics integration is deferred to future work, so the practical claims are partially speculative.

The manuscript has presentation defects: raw LaTeX source is visible in Equations (1)–(3) and supplementary equations, indicating a careless submission; the 'we are the first' claim is not carefully substantiated against active-perception literature the authors themselves cite.

strengths: The 'diagnose-then-rectify' paradigm is a clear and well-motivated conceptual shift from passive view-selection to active verification: comparing passive crop captions against a caption from a synthetically rendered optimal viewpoint is a sensible and novel way to quantify semantic ambiguity in cross-view aggregation, and positions the work well against passive frame-selection methods (BBQ, MomaGraph).

Comprehensive and largely convincing empirical evidence: state-of-the-art comparisons on two challenging real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D) under the OpenFunGraph protocol, a well-specified human evaluation on Replica with an explicit annotation protocol and Fleiss' Kappa (κ=0.76), component ablations (Fig. 3, Tab. 3), pose-noise stress tests, and an actual robotic deployment. The analysis variants (Passive VLM, Re-shot VLM, Ours Node + CG Edge) are particularly valuable because they isolate where the gains come from (node quality drives edge gains), showing the authors understand their own system.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough and materially improves reproducibility: hyperparameter sweeps with justified (not cherry-picked) choices, qualitative ablation of re-shot scoring weights showing failure modes, density stress tests, pseudo-code for fusion, and complete prompt templates.

The system demonstrates practical awareness: runtime/cost analysis (~$0.50/scene API cost, ~0.26s/object rendering overhead), fast downsampling that accelerates fusion 6.65s→2.49s, and a local LLaVA variant showing the framework is not merely a GPT-4o wrapper (Ours-LLaVA already surpasses the previous SOTA).
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on prompt engineering and heuristic design choices rather than principled uncertainty estimation: the uncertainty score is a CLIP caption-similarity statistic (KMeans with K=3, consensus cluster mean), a hard 50% low-uncertainty cutoff, a nearest-neighbor 'semantic anchor' retriever, and hand-designed prioritized rules for caption arbitration. This works empirically but is brittle, dataset-specific, and offers limited theoretical grounding for what 'uncertainty' actually measures (a single re-shot caption is itself a noisy sample, and the paper does not analyze the reliability of this proxy).

The claimed 'open-vocabulary' edge space is contradicted by the method: Sec. 3.3 deliberately constrains relations to eight predefined categories with few-shot examples. This is defensible for stability, but it weakens the framing that the contribution retains an open relation space and complicates comparison fairness, even with the BERT-based mapping protocol of OpenFunGraph.

Some framing is overstated relative to what is done. The 'active photographer' narrative suggests physically re-observing the scene, but all re-shots are virtual renders from the reconstructed (already fused) point cloud; thus the method cannot recover information that the reconstruction lost, and the 'w/ Noisy Pose' robustness result partly follows from the VLM falling back to uncorrupted 2D crops — i.e., the strong robustness is partly a property of crop retention rather than of the re-shot mechanism. Also, GPT-4o-based headline numbers benefit from a much stronger backend than most baselines; the LLaVA variant partially mitigates this, but backbone confounds across baselines (e.g., ConceptGraphs) are not fully controlled.

Equations and notation have typographical/formatting issues (Eq. 1 rendered as raw LaTeX in places, the 'Passive VLM (gpt-5.2)' label is confusing, 'Ours Node + CG Edge' has missing node columns in Tab. 1), and hyperparameters like δsim=0.45 are selected partly on the same Replica evaluation set used for ablations, raising mild evaluation leakage concerns.

No code release is mentioned, and the pipeline stacks many interacting components (SAM, CLIP, VLM, LLM, rendering, KMeans clustering); without release, exact reproduction of the reported gains would be difficult. The societal discussion is limited to a brief motivating example rather than a treatment of risks of VLM-based rectification (e.g., hallucinated 'corrections' in safety-critical contexts).
